def: Re-running the original analysis on the original data to check you get the same numbers.
Repeating a study as exactly as possible with new data, to test whether the original result holds.
Testing the same idea with deliberately different methods, measures or samples, to see whether it generalises.
The FORRT Replication Database: a searchable list of replication studies and their outcomes.
A number for how big an effect is (e.g. Cohen's d or a correlation r), independent of sample size.
A range of plausible values for the true effect. Narrow intervals mean a precise estimate.
The chance that a study detects an effect of a given size if it really exists. A power analysis tells you how many participants you need.
A sample-size approach: test whether the original study could even have detected the effect. A common rule of thumb is about 2.5 times the original sample.
The smallest effect you would still consider meaningful. You need it to show that an effect is absent or negligible.
A test of whether an effect is small enough to count as negligible, i.e. inside a range you set in advance (two one-sided tests, TOST).
Accuracy in parameter estimation: planning the sample so the confidence interval around the effect is narrow enough.
A number expressing how much more the data support one hypothesis (e.g. 'no effect') than another.
Evidence that a measure really captures what it claims to, e.g. reliability, factor structure, or correlations with related measures.
How consistently a measure gives similar scores. Cronbach's α is a common index, but on its own it does not show validity.
Whether a questionnaire's items group together in the way the theory expects (checked with factor analysis).
Whether a questionnaire works the same way in different groups or languages, so scores can be compared.
A question or measure confirming that the experimental manipulation worked as intended.
An item that identifies participants who are not reading carefully, e.g. 'Please select 3 for this question'.

A starting number for a computer's random-number generator. Setting it makes analyses that use randomness (e.g. bootstrapping) give the same result every time. If your analysis uses no randomness, you can ignore it.
Checking whether a result still holds after small, reasonable changes to the analysis (e.g. a different outlier rule).
A time-stamped public record of your hypotheses and analysis plan, made before you collect or look at the data.
A paper format where the introduction and methods are peer-reviewed and accepted before data collection, so publication doesn't depend on the results.
Rules, set in advance, for which participants or data points are left out of the analysis.
What you will do if something goes wrong, decided in advance.
Working with researchers who expect a different result, agreeing the design in advance so both sides accept the outcome.
A website where researchers comment on published papers. Useful for finding known problems with your target study.
A free platform for sharing materials, data and code, and for preregistering studies.
How much a replication could add: high when the result matters AND we are still unsure whether it is true.
Any way in which what you actually did differs from what you preregistered. Report all of them openly.
